top_news.title: HONG KONG RADIOLOGIST ADVOCATES HUMAN-CENTRED AI AT UN HUMAN RIGHTS COUNCIL IN GENEVA
top_news.summary: Dr. Kevin Lau Chung-hang welcomes deepening Medical AI: AI for Diagnostic Precision, Doctors for Compassionate Care GENEVA and HONG KONG, Sept. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Speaking at the 63rd Session of the United Nations Human Rights Council (HRC63) at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, Dr. Kevin Lau Chung-hang (MH, awarded the Medal of Honour by the HKSAR Government in 2023) delivered a speech calling for the compassionate and equitable deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) to address global development disparities. This marks Dr. Lau's fourth address to the Human Rights Council, having previously attended its 49th, 50th and 58th sessions. This year marks the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Declaration on the Right to Development and the 60th anniversary of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights - two major milestones on the international human rights agenda, giving special significance to this session of the Council. Dr. Lau, a practising radiologist, the Founder & Senior Advisor of Trinity Medical Group and Founding Convenor of the Hong Kong Youth Professional Global Advocacy (HKYPGA), addressed a side event titled "AI for a Better Future." The session was co-hosted by the Permanent Mission of the People's Republic of China to the UN Office at Geneva and the China NGO Network for International Exchanges (CNIE). Download for images and videos Bridging Healthcare and Digital Divides Drawing from his frontline experience in Hong Kong's public hospitals, Dr. Lau noted how AI is already transforming local care. Hong Kong's Hospital Authority currently operates 15 AI models across public hospitals, including automated systems that triage 2,000 chest X-rays daily. However, Dr. Lau stressed that technological progress must serve human dignity. "AI will read the scan; the doctor must still hold the hand," he stated, pointing out that intelligence without compassion remains mere computation. He highlighted critical global workforce shortages, citing World Health Organization projections of a 10 million health worker deficit by 2030. In the WHO African Region, the current workforce meets just 43 per cent of demand, with nations like Ghana having only three radiologists per million people. Meanwhile, 2.2 billion people remain offline globally, further widening inequalities. To address these gaps, Dr. Lau pointed to practical solutions, including portable AI medical-imaging units developed in China weighing under 25 kg. Deployed in rural Kyrgyzstan, now delivering rapid tuberculosis screenings for up to 400 patients per day, with each scan completed in just 15 seconds. To support global capability building, Dr. Lau highlighted that China's frontier AI models are "open-weight" and can be downloaded and deployed at a fraction of the cost. He also noted key international initiatives, including the World AI Cooperation Organisation (WAICO) - the world's first intergovernmental organisation dedicated to AI cooperation, headquartered in Shanghai. He further cited the WAIC Chairman's Statement, which prioritises the Global South, alongside UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, which places human rights and human dignity at the centre. Hong Kong's Role as a Global Hub Dr. Lau emphasised Hong Kong's role as a bridge for international cooperation. He highlighted the Cyberport's Artificial Intelligence Supercomputing Centre (AISC), which is scaling up toward 3,000 petaflops, alongside the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster ranked as the world's No. 1 Global Innovation Cluster for the second consecutive year in WIPO's Global Innovation Index. Echoing the Right to Development under Item 3 of the Council's agenda, Dr. Lau concluded: "Development is not a favour granted by the strong. No child offline, no patient unseen, no nation left behind." Other speech: Development dignity Dr. Lau asserted that human rights must be measured by tangible improvements in ordinary lives. Drawing a parallel between reading medical scans and evaluating human welfare, he emphasised prioritising life first, arguing that economic vitality serves as the foundational bedrock of human rights and dignity. Highlighting Hong Kong's stability and economic growth under "One Country, Two Systems," Dr. Lau cited key "vital signs," including the city's top-tier global competitiveness rankings, leading innovation cluster status in the Greater Bay Area, and robust financial market performance. He stressed that economic opportunity empowers youth and protects the vulnerable by turning rights into lived reality. Dr. Lau concluded by calling on the Council to favour constructive dialogue and international cooperation over confrontation and "naming-and-shaming," urging nations to advance the global right to development together. Other speech: From Historical Denial to Judicial Due Process: A Universal Human Rights Standard Addressing the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, Dr. Lau advocates for a unified, non-selective standard of human rights accountability. Speaking as a father, he criticises Japan for failing to provide statistical data, investigate crimes, or allow victim memorials concerning the arbitrary detention of "comfort women" eighty years after the Tokyo Trials, describing historical denial as a "second detention." Transitioning to local governance, Dr. Lau defends Hong Kong's legal system, asserting that its courts operate independently under the Basic Law and international covenants. Ultimately, Dr. Lau calls on the Council to operate without selectivity - urging equal commitment to prevention, investigation, and remembrance to enable genuine global healing. Other speech: One Standard of Liberty Addressing arbitrary detention as a global scourge, Dr. Lau called for non-selective oversight, asserting: "So we speak truth in love - and we hold ourselves to the same light." Speaking as a father, he condemned Japan's ongoing failure to account for or investigate its historical enslavement of "comfort women", stating: "Every one of those girls was somebody's daughter." He expressed deep outrage over Tokyo's historical revisionism, adding: "What was done to them disgusts me; the denial disgusts me more" and warning that "Denial is the second detention." Dr. Lau emphasised that Hong Kong remains firmly underpinned by an independent rule of law, with residents' rights fully protected under the Basic Law and international covenants. Stressing that judicial outcomes are based on rigorous evidence rather than opinion. He concluded by urging the Council to operate without selectivity, calling for impartial oversight and a collaborative approach to international peacemaking and healing. Other speech: IPLSA Forum "84 Seconds to Midnight" Marking the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, Dr. Lau urged Japan to fully confront its wartime legacy and halt rapid remilitarisation. He warned that historical denial poses a direct threat to regional peace. He detailed World War II atrocities, including theNanjing Massacre, Unit 731, and the system of "comfort women", criticising Tokyo's historical whitewashing as a deliberate policy choice rather than a failure of memory. He cautioned that unaddressed past aggression licenses present military expansion. Citing Japan's doubling defence spending and Sanae Takaichi's rhetoric that "a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency," he described these trends as dangerous erosion of its peace constitution and the UN Charter. Dr. Lau called on Tokyo to abandon historical revisionism, accept postwar outcomes, and re-embrace peaceful diplomacy. He emphasised that "those who cannot face history should not be trusted with missiles," and warned that "a nation that rewrites its past is rehearsing its future." top_news.title: Nepal PM Shah prioritises disaster early warning systems after devastating Bhotekoshi floods
top_news.summary: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Saturday announced that disaster early warning systems will be implemented with the highest priority, following the devastating floods in the country's Bhotekoshi and Trishuli River basins that caused extensive loss of life and infrastructure damage. Addressing the nation on the occasion of Constitution Day, Shah said Nepal must adopt a proactive approach to disaster management, with greater emphasis on risk reduction, preparedness and response. "The damage caused by the recent Rasuwa- Bhotekoshi floods has been unimaginable and irreparable for us. At this critical juncture, I extend my special thanks and gratitude to all friendly nations, the international community and organisations, the private sector, civil servants, and the general public for their assistance in rescue operations and contributions to relief efforts," Shah said. He further said Nepal's vulnerability to disasters requires the country to strengthen its preparedness before disasters strike. "Nepal is among the countries at high risk of disasters globally. We address this reality proactively-before a disaster strikes, rather than after the fact. Special emphasis will be placed on risk reduction, preparedness, and response. Disaster early warning systems will be implemented with the highest priority," the Nepal Prime Minister added. Shah delivered the address for the first time on Constitution Day since assuming office in March this year. A special ceremony was held at the Army Pavilion to mark the promulgation of Nepal's Constitution through the Constituent Assembly on September 20, 2015. The Constitution was promulgated following a prolonged political transition and the country's peace process. It formally established Nepal as a federal democratic republic, replacing the previous unitary system and ending the monarchy. The Constitution provides for a three-tier system of government comprising the federal government, seven provinces and 753 local levels. It also guarantees political, economic, social and cultural rights and provides for the distribution of powers among the three levels of government. This year's Constitution Day celebrations come as Nepal continues to deal with the aftermath of a major disaster that affected several districts of the Himalayan nation. A flash flood struck riverside settlements in Rasuwa district on August 26, rapidly affecting neighbouring areas including Nuwakot and Dhading. According to the latest figures from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 13,756 people have been rescued, while 6,055 remain out of contact. A total of 1,410 bodies have been recovered, of which several have been identified and handed over to their families. Of the 344 injured people admitted to hospitals, 290 have since been discharged, according to the figures. The Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force launched a large-scale response following the disaster, with the number of security personnel deployed at one point exceeding 20,000. Helicopter operations focused on evacuating critically injured people, pregnant women, children, elderly persons and people with disabilities. Temporary shelters have been established at 13 locations in Nuwakot, housing 611 people. The disaster also caused extensive damage to infrastructure and the energy sector. Eight operating hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 281 MW and four projects under construction with a combined capacity of 388 MW were damaged, affecting 431.1 MW of generation capacity. Major sections of the Galchhi-Betrawati-Rasuwagadhi road and the Prithvi Highway were also destroyed or severely damaged, along with 48 suspension bridges and 31 motorable bridges. Telecommunications services have been restored across 95 per cent of the affected areas, while electricity restoration has progressed at different rates across the affected districts. Shah also acknowledged international support following the disaster, noting that Nepal had received messages of goodwill and material assistance from countries and multilateral partners, including India, China, the United States, Japan, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank, the European Union and the United Nations. The government has declared 15 local levels as disaster crisis-hit areas for three months and released funds from the Prime Minister's Relief Fund, which has collected more than NPR 7 billion in addition to foreign contributions. Authorities have begun immediate relief operations alongside longer-term recovery efforts, including road restoration and bridge reconstruction. Search operations for missing people are continuing, while unidentified bodies are being handled through scientific procedures, with DNA samples preserved for identification. Against the backdrop of the disaster's heavy human and economic toll, Shah's Constitution Day address placed renewed emphasis on strengthening Nepal's disaster preparedness and establishing early warning systems as a priority. top_news.title: Nandigram Bypoll: Congress Candidate Milan Pradhan produced before court after arrest in 2007 cases; party alleges vendetta
top_news.summary: Congress candidate from Nandigram Assembly bypoll Milan Pradhan was produced before a court on Saturday following his arrest in connection with pending cases dating back to the 2007 Nandigram anti-land acquisition movement, with the party alleging a political vendetta behind the action. Pradhan and Pradesh Congress Secretary Subhashis Bhattacharya were arrested in Chandipur amid heightened political activity in the constituency ahead of the October 6 bypoll. Bhattacharya was arrested for allegedly obstructing police from apprehending Pradhan, according to Congress leaders. Speaking to ANI on Pradhan's arrest, AICC In-Charge for West Bengal Prakash Joshi alleged that the action was linked to political reasons and claimed that Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee's faction extending support to the Congress candidate had led to the development. "The moment Congress fielded Milan Pradhan-who was a key figure in the 2007 Nandigram land acquisition movement-the Chief Minister was bound to feel threatened. After all, Suvendu Adhikari was also part of that movement and is well aware of Milan Pradhan's strength. He has been apprehensive ever since, realising that the election outcome could go either way," Joshi said. "This explains the situation regarding a case stemming from a political vendetta during that movement; while Suvendu Adhikari-who was part of the then-ruling TMC-managed to get his own cases dropped, Milan Pradhan was under the impression that his case was also closed, believing the government wouldn't lie. Trusting this, he didn't pursue the matter further, only for the case to be suddenly reopened and for him to be jailed," he added. Joshi further alleged that Pradhan was targeted because he was a strong contender in the bypoll. "I don't view it as an arrest made after receiving support. I believe Suvendu Adhikari had planned this all along, knowing that Milan Pradhan was a formidable candidate. He was tortured that night; the police pressured him to withdraw and even tried to bribe him, but he refused to yield. What could be more significant than that? That is his strength," he said. Bhattacharya, while describing the incident, said he was present at a house in the area where Pradhan was staying when police arrived. "I was sleeping at the house when I suddenly heard someone shouting loudly. Milan Pradhan, who was at the same house, called out to me by my nickname and asked me for help, saying that police were taking him away," he said. Pradhan was arrested in connection with pending cases related to the 2007 Nandigram anti-land acquisition movement. According to reports, police executed a pending warrant in a murder case linked to the agitation. He has been named in multiple cases connected with the movement. The arrest was made on Friday hours after former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee announced that her faction would support Pradhan in the Nandigram bypoll after its candidate Sanchita Pradhan Dey withdrew from the contest. Banerjee questioned the timing of the arrest, alleging that an old case was revived after her faction extended support to the Congress candidate. The Congress also questioned the timing of the police action, pointing out that the cases date back to 2007. West Bengal Congress president Subhankar Sarkar said the party was initially unaware of the reason behind Pradhan's arrest and his whereabouts. The BJP has rejected allegations of political interference and maintained that the police action was carried out as per law. A police officer cited in reports said the arrest was related to a pending warrant in a 2007 murder case and such warrants are executed irrespective of elections. The Nandigram Assembly bypoll is scheduled for October 6, while counting of votes will take place on October 9. (ANI)

articles.title: HONG KONG RADIOLOGIST ADVOCATES HUMAN-CENTRED AI AT UN HUMAN RIGHTS COUNCIL IN GENEVA
articles.summary: Dr. Kevin Lau Chung-hang welcomes deepening Medical AI: AI for Diagnostic Precision, Doctors for Compassionate Care GENEVA and HONG KONG, Sept. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Speaking at the 63rd Session of the United Nations Human Rights Council (HRC63) at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, Dr. Kevin Lau Chung-hang (MH, awarded the Medal of Honour by the HKSAR Government in 2023) delivered a speech calling for the compassionate and equitable deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) to address global development disparities. This marks Dr. Lau's fourth address to the Human Rights Council, having previously attended its 49th, 50th and 58th sessions. This year marks the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Declaration on the Right to Development and the 60th anniversary of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights - two major milestones on the international human rights agenda, giving special significance to this session of the Council. Dr. Lau, a practising radiologist, the Founder & Senior Advisor of Trinity Medical Group and Founding Convenor of the Hong Kong Youth Professional Global Advocacy (HKYPGA), addressed a side event titled "AI for a Better Future." The session was co-hosted by the Permanent Mission of the People's Republic of China to the UN Office at Geneva and the China NGO Network for International Exchanges (CNIE). Download for images and videos Bridging Healthcare and Digital Divides Drawing from his frontline experience in Hong Kong's public hospitals, Dr. Lau noted how AI is already transforming local care. Hong Kong's Hospital Authority currently operates 15 AI models across public hospitals, including automated systems that triage 2,000 chest X-rays daily. However, Dr. Lau stressed that technological progress must serve human dignity. "AI will read the scan; the doctor must still hold the hand," he stated, pointing out that intelligence without compassion remains mere computation. He highlighted critical global workforce shortages, citing World Health Organization projections of a 10 million health worker deficit by 2030. In the WHO African Region, the current workforce meets just 43 per cent of demand, with nations like Ghana having only three radiologists per million people. Meanwhile, 2.2 billion people remain offline globally, further widening inequalities. To address these gaps, Dr. Lau pointed to practical solutions, including portable AI medical-imaging units developed in China weighing under 25 kg. Deployed in rural Kyrgyzstan, now delivering rapid tuberculosis screenings for up to 400 patients per day, with each scan completed in just 15 seconds. To support global capability building, Dr. Lau highlighted that China's frontier AI models are "open-weight" and can be downloaded and deployed at a fraction of the cost. He also noted key international initiatives, including the World AI Cooperation Organisation (WAICO) - the world's first intergovernmental organisation dedicated to AI cooperation, headquartered in Shanghai. He further cited the WAIC Chairman's Statement, which prioritises the Global South, alongside UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, which places human rights and human dignity at the centre. Hong Kong's Role as a Global Hub Dr. Lau emphasised Hong Kong's role as a bridge for international cooperation. He highlighted the Cyberport's Artificial Intelligence Supercomputing Centre (AISC), which is scaling up toward 3,000 petaflops, alongside the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster ranked as the world's No. 1 Global Innovation Cluster for the second consecutive year in WIPO's Global Innovation Index. Echoing the Right to Development under Item 3 of the Council's agenda, Dr. Lau concluded: "Development is not a favour granted by the strong. No child offline, no patient unseen, no nation left behind." Other speech: Development dignity Dr. Lau asserted that human rights must be measured by tangible improvements in ordinary lives. Drawing a parallel between reading medical scans and evaluating human welfare, he emphasised prioritising life first, arguing that economic vitality serves as the foundational bedrock of human rights and dignity. Highlighting Hong Kong's stability and economic growth under "One Country, Two Systems," Dr. Lau cited key "vital signs," including the city's top-tier global competitiveness rankings, leading innovation cluster status in the Greater Bay Area, and robust financial market performance. He stressed that economic opportunity empowers youth and protects the vulnerable by turning rights into lived reality. Dr. Lau concluded by calling on the Council to favour constructive dialogue and international cooperation over confrontation and "naming-and-shaming," urging nations to advance the global right to development together. Other speech: From Historical Denial to Judicial Due Process: A Universal Human Rights Standard Addressing the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, Dr. Lau advocates for a unified, non-selective standard of human rights accountability. Speaking as a father, he criticises Japan for failing to provide statistical data, investigate crimes, or allow victim memorials concerning the arbitrary detention of "comfort women" eighty years after the Tokyo Trials, describing historical denial as a "second detention." Transitioning to local governance, Dr. Lau defends Hong Kong's legal system, asserting that its courts operate independently under the Basic Law and international covenants. Ultimately, Dr. Lau calls on the Council to operate without selectivity - urging equal commitment to prevention, investigation, and remembrance to enable genuine global healing. Other speech: One Standard of Liberty Addressing arbitrary detention as a global scourge, Dr. Lau called for non-selective oversight, asserting: "So we speak truth in love - and we hold ourselves to the same light." Speaking as a father, he condemned Japan's ongoing failure to account for or investigate its historical enslavement of "comfort women", stating: "Every one of those girls was somebody's daughter." He expressed deep outrage over Tokyo's historical revisionism, adding: "What was done to them disgusts me; the denial disgusts me more" and warning that "Denial is the second detention." Dr. Lau emphasised that Hong Kong remains firmly underpinned by an independent rule of law, with residents' rights fully protected under the Basic Law and international covenants. Stressing that judicial outcomes are based on rigorous evidence rather than opinion. He concluded by urging the Council to operate without selectivity, calling for impartial oversight and a collaborative approach to international peacemaking and healing. Other speech: IPLSA Forum "84 Seconds to Midnight" Marking the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, Dr. Lau urged Japan to fully confront its wartime legacy and halt rapid remilitarisation. He warned that historical denial poses a direct threat to regional peace. He detailed World War II atrocities, including theNanjing Massacre, Unit 731, and the system of "comfort women", criticising Tokyo's historical whitewashing as a deliberate policy choice rather than a failure of memory. He cautioned that unaddressed past aggression licenses present military expansion. Citing Japan's doubling defence spending and Sanae Takaichi's rhetoric that "a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency," he described these trends as dangerous erosion of its peace constitution and the UN Charter. Dr. Lau called on Tokyo to abandon historical revisionism, accept postwar outcomes, and re-embrace peaceful diplomacy. He emphasised that "those who cannot face history should not be trusted with missiles," and warned that "a nation that rewrites its past is rehearsing its future." He takes deep interest in the development of medical affairs in Hong Kong. Lau has been recently appointed as the Community Service Advisor of The Life Underwriters Association of Hong Kong and the Honorary Medical Advisor of Junior Police Officers' Association. Dr. Lau is an active member of several governmental and medical bodies. articles.title: Nepal PM Shah prioritises disaster early warning systems after devastating Bhotekoshi floods
articles.summary: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Saturday announced that disaster early warning systems will be implemented with the highest priority, following the devastating floods in the country's Bhotekoshi and Trishuli River basins that caused extensive loss of life and infrastructure damage. Addressing the nation on the occasion of Constitution Day, Shah said Nepal must adopt a proactive approach to disaster management, with greater emphasis on risk reduction, preparedness and response. "The damage caused by the recent Rasuwa- Bhotekoshi floods has been unimaginable and irreparable for us. At this critical juncture, I extend my special thanks and gratitude to all friendly nations, the international community and organisations, the private sector, civil servants, and the general public for their assistance in rescue operations and contributions to relief efforts," Shah said. He further said Nepal's vulnerability to disasters requires the country to strengthen its preparedness before disasters strike. "Nepal is among the countries at high risk of disasters globally. We address this reality proactively-before a disaster strikes, rather than after the fact. Special emphasis will be placed on risk reduction, preparedness, and response. Disaster early warning systems will be implemented with the highest priority," the Nepal Prime Minister added. Shah delivered the address for the first time on Constitution Day since assuming office in March this year. A special ceremony was held at the Army Pavilion to mark the promulgation of Nepal's Constitution through the Constituent Assembly on September 20, 2015. The Constitution was promulgated following a prolonged political transition and the country's peace process. It formally established Nepal as a federal democratic republic, replacing the previous unitary system and ending the monarchy. The Constitution provides for a three-tier system of government comprising the federal government, seven provinces and 753 local levels. It also guarantees political, economic, social and cultural rights and provides for the distribution of powers among the three levels of government. This year's Constitution Day celebrations come as Nepal continues to deal with the aftermath of a major disaster that affected several districts of the Himalayan nation. A flash flood struck riverside settlements in Rasuwa district on August 26, rapidly affecting neighbouring areas including Nuwakot and Dhading. According to the latest figures from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 13,756 people have been rescued, while 6,055 remain out of contact. A total of 1,410 bodies have been recovered, of which several have been identified and handed over to their families. Of the 344 injured people admitted to hospitals, 290 have since been discharged, according to the figures. The Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force launched a large-scale response following the disaster, with the number of security personnel deployed at one point exceeding 20,000. Helicopter operations focused on evacuating critically injured people, pregnant women, children, elderly persons and people with disabilities. Temporary shelters have been established at 13 locations in Nuwakot, housing 611 people. The disaster also caused extensive damage to infrastructure and the energy sector. Eight operating hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 281 MW and four projects under construction with a combined capacity of 388 MW were damaged, affecting 431.1 MW of generation capacity. Major sections of the Galchhi-Betrawati-Rasuwagadhi road and the Prithvi Highway were also destroyed or severely damaged, along with 48 suspension bridges and 31 motorable bridges. Telecommunications services have been restored across 95 per cent of the affected areas, while electricity restoration has progressed at different rates across the affected districts. Shah also acknowledged international support following the disaster, noting that Nepal had received messages of goodwill and material assistance from countries and multilateral partners, including India, China, the United States, Japan, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank, the European Union and the United Nations. The government has declared 15 local levels as disaster crisis-hit areas for three months and released funds from the Prime Minister's Relief Fund, which has collected more than NPR 7 billion in addition to foreign contributions. Authorities have begun immediate relief operations alongside longer-term recovery efforts, including road restoration and bridge reconstruction. Search operations for missing people are continuing, while unidentified bodies are being handled through scientific procedures, with DNA samples preserved for identification. Against the backdrop of the disaster's heavy human and economic toll, Shah's Constitution Day address placed renewed emphasis on strengthening Nepal's disaster preparedness and establishing early warning systems as a priority. (ANI)

articles.title: Nandigram Bypoll: Congress Candidate Milan Pradhan produced before court after arrest in 2007 cases; party alleges vendetta
articles.summary: Congress candidate from Nandigram Assembly bypoll Milan Pradhan was produced before a court on Saturday following his arrest in connection with pending cases dating back to the 2007 Nandigram anti-land acquisition movement, with the party alleging a political vendetta behind the action. Pradhan and Pradesh Congress Secretary Subhashis Bhattacharya were arrested in Chandipur amid heightened political activity in the constituency ahead of the October 6 bypoll. Bhattacharya was arrested for allegedly obstructing police from apprehending Pradhan, according to Congress leaders. Speaking to ANI on Pradhan's arrest, AICC In-Charge for West Bengal Prakash Joshi alleged that the action was linked to political reasons and claimed that Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee's faction extending support to the Congress candidate had led to the development. "The moment Congress fielded Milan Pradhan-who was a key figure in the 2007 Nandigram land acquisition movement-the Chief Minister was bound to feel threatened. After all, Suvendu Adhikari was also part of that movement and is well aware of Milan Pradhan's strength. He has been apprehensive ever since, realising that the election outcome could go either way," Joshi said. "This explains the situation regarding a case stemming from a political vendetta during that movement; while Suvendu Adhikari-who was part of the then-ruling TMC-managed to get his own cases dropped, Milan Pradhan was under the impression that his case was also closed, believing the government wouldn't lie. Trusting this, he didn't pursue the matter further, only for the case to be suddenly reopened and for him to be jailed," he added. Joshi further alleged that Pradhan was targeted because he was a strong contender in the bypoll. "I don't view it as an arrest made after receiving support. I believe Suvendu Adhikari had planned this all along, knowing that Milan Pradhan was a formidable candidate. He was tortured that night; the police pressured him to withdraw and even tried to bribe him, but he refused to yield. What could be more significant than that? That is his strength," he said. Bhattacharya, while describing the incident, said he was present at a house in the area where Pradhan was staying when police arrived. "I was sleeping at the house when I suddenly heard someone shouting loudly. Milan Pradhan, who was at the same house, called out to me by my nickname and asked me for help, saying that police were taking him away," he said. Pradhan was arrested in connection with pending cases related to the 2007 Nandigram anti-land acquisition movement. According to reports, police executed a pending warrant in a murder case linked to the agitation. He has been named in multiple cases connected with the movement. The arrest was made on Friday hours after former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee announced that her faction would support Pradhan in the Nandigram bypoll after its candidate Sanchita Pradhan Dey withdrew from the contest. Banerjee questioned the timing of the arrest, alleging that an old case was revived after her faction extended support to the Congress candidate. The Congress also questioned the timing of the police action, pointing out that the cases date back to 2007. West Bengal Congress president Subhankar Sarkar said the party was initially unaware of the reason behind Pradhan's arrest and his whereabouts. The BJP has rejected allegations of political interference and maintained that the police action was carried out as per law. A police officer cited in reports said the arrest was related to a pending warrant in a 2007 murder case and such warrants are executed irrespective of elections. The Nandigram Assembly bypoll is scheduled for October 6, while counting of votes will take place on October 9. (ANI)
